title: By the rivers of Babylon (Psalm 136 [137])
hook: exiles weep, and the last verse is raw rage; the Church keeps it honest, not as a command

segments.voice: Yesterday, like a weaned child: a soul content to be held. Your line was quieted. What did you put down? Today the quiet breaks. This one is raw. Day one hundred eighty-nine.

There's a reggae song with these words, and later a dance-floor hit. Bright, bouncy, easy to sing along to. The words come from a psalm. And the psalm is no party. It's a group of exiles sitting beside foreign rivers, far from home. Their city has been burned. Their Temple is gone. And the people who carried them off stand over them and say: go on, sing us one of the songs of Sion. Today: by the rivers of Babylon.
screen: `A SONG FROM THE RADIO.` → `EXILES BY FOREIGN RIVERS.` → `SING US ONE OF THE SONGS OF SION.`

segments.voice: First, the history. The Babylonian army destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple, and carried many of its people away to Babylon. This psalm is their voice. In the Douay-Rheims: "Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept: when we remembered Sion." They hang their instruments on the willows. Then the taunt comes, and their answer: "How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a strange land?" Second, the vow. If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, the psalmist says, let my right hand be forgotten. Jews have kept that vow close, and one explanation given for the glass broken at a Jewish wedding is to remember Jerusalem even in the middle of joy. Third, the ending, which is hard to hear. The last verse blesses whoever would take Babylon's little ones and dash them against the rock. There's no softening it. It's the voice of people who watched their own city fall. So what does the Church do with that? It doesn't pretend the verse isn't there. It keeps it in the Bible as an honest cry, not as a command. The psalmist doesn't act on it; he says it to God. In the Liturgy of the Hours, the Church leaves those last verses out of common prayer. And some of the old monks read them another way: Saint Benedict, in his Rule, speaks of dashing evil thoughts against Christ, the rock, while they're still small. So the psalm shows something surprising: the Bible lets people bring even their worst anger into prayer.
screen: `THE CITY BURNED, THE PEOPLE TAKEN.` · `IF I FORGET THEE, O JERUSALEM.` · `THE LAST VERSE: RAW RAGE.` · `KEPT HONEST, NOT A COMMAND.` · then, large: `HOW SHALL WE SING THE SONG OF THE LORD?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring your anger honestly. Settle, and breathe. Let yourself notice one thing you're angry about. Something done to you, or to someone you love, or something in the news. Don't dress it up. Name it plainly, in your head. If you pray, you can hand it to God as it is, rough and unfinished, the way the psalmist did. If you don't pray, just let yourself feel it without acting on it, and breathe out slowly. The bell holds the time.
By the rivers of Babylon. The song of exiles weeping for Jerusalem, whose last verse is rage handed over to God. Today's word.
screen: `BY THE RIVERS OF BABYLON — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: even anger can be prayed. This week took us from a lamp to our feet, up the pilgrim road, into Jerusalem's gates, out of the depths, to a quiet lap, and now to the rivers of exile. Today, when anger comes, say it to God or to the quiet before you say it to anyone else. Day one hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 136 [137] in the Liturgy of the Hours without its final verses, and read the whole psalm in scripture as the lament of the exiles.

original.note: Latin: upon the rivers of Babylon, the psalm's first words in the Vulgate.

trapdoor: what you thought: a song from the radio.
what it means: refugees grieving a destroyed city, bringing even their rage to God instead of acting on it.
what a scholar hears: the Babylonian exile; an imprecatory ending omitted from the Liturgy of the Hours and read allegorically in the Rule of Benedict.

notes: Douay-Rheims 136:1 and 136:4 given from memory; confirm.
Date of Jerusalem's destruction: 587 or 586 BC (scholars differ); the script says 587.
The Melodians' 'Rivers of Babylon' (1970) and the Boney M. cover (1978): mentioned without naming or quoting.
Liturgy of the Hours omits verses 7–9 of this psalm (per the General Instruction's policy on imprecatory verses, GILH 131); confirm the exact omitted verses.
Rule of Benedict, Prologue 28, reads Psalm 137:9 allegorically (dash thoughts against Christ); Augustine reads it similarly. Confirm.
Breaking a glass at Jewish weddings to remember Jerusalem's destruction: a common explanation among several; stated as 'at many Jewish weddings'.
